correctness.rationale: The finite state space has exactly 512 color masks, nine ant positions and four headings. The time-one map has an explicit inverse. The source file cover_certificate.py independently validates all 72 symmetry commutations, primitive periods of eight representatives, disjointness and exact covering of all 18,432 states with the claimed period-specific orbit counts. exhaustive_cycles.cpp separately traces every state and independently inverts the map, reproducing the complete table. Both actual output files are included. No sample-to-infinite inference is used.

evidence: Gale et al. 1995 prove planar Truchet-tile statements for generalized ant rule strings and explicitly note the failure of a key planar argument on tori (arXiv:math/9501233v1, section 4).
Tsukiji–Hagiwara 2011 obtain complexity bounds for reversible generalized ants on infinite square/hexagonal lattices, DOI:10.3390/a4010001, sections 1–2 and theorem statements.
The earlier 2-by-n Langton-ant orbit theorem applies to a two-row torus, not the 3-by-3 torus.
broader_coverage.reasoning: These are broader contexts or related families, but none provides a 3-by-3 all-state cycle decomposition with the claimed symmetry classes. The previously treated 2-by-n grid has geometrically identified opposite vertical neighbours, unlike a 3-by-3 grid.

Those quantities require the new exhaustive covering certificate. Conversely, the presence of one known 66-cycle is consistent with many different unknown remaining cycle decompositions.

evidence: The 1995 preprint describes the two-colour ant with cell-entry turns and bit flipping, arXiv:math/9501233v1, sections 2–4.

equivalent_formulations.reasoning: The proposed census is invariant under one-step time re-indexing and under global colour inversion followed by reflection. Prior formulations of the standard ant describe the same dynamics but do not give its complete 3-by-3 permutation or cycle counts. The known 66-step full return is explicitly included rather than treated as novel.

evidence: OEIS A386970 tabulates special all-white 3-by-n return periods, including 66 at n=3, not all 18,432 starting states.
The 2019 Mathematics Stack Exchange answer gives a rectangular-torus table for the all-white initial state; for 3-by-3 it reports 66 and three quasi-recurrences.
No inspected table lists the full period spectrum 18, 30, 42, 66, 70, 74, 78, 102 and the vector of primitive-orbit counts.
exact_database_or_table.reasoning: The strongest tabular match fixes one orbit period, 66, already credited. A single special-state return cannot determine the complete finite permutation, its other cycle lengths, multiplicities, or spatial-symmetry structure.

originality.rationale: Neither the fully inspected 1995 paper nor the 2011 generalized-ant paper concerns the exact all-state dynamics on the finite 3-by-3 torus. The 2019 torus discussion and later OEIS entry give the period 66 of an all-white special initial state, as well as general symmetries, but not the other seven periods, the numbers of primitive cycles, or the demonstration that their 288 cycles form precisely eight extended symmetry orbits. Own available earlier research gives an all-n census on the 2-by-n band, with different geometry, so it does not imply this 3-by-3 classification. Relevant published-record searches found no exact covering result; unindexed prior enumerations remain possible.
residual_risks: No exhaustive search can exclude nonindexed unpublished or privately circulated complete 3-by-3 orbit enumerations.
The scientific conclusion depends on the correctness of the two fully inspectable finite-state programs and their stated operation convention.
No independent external expert audit has yet been completed.

value.rationale: The first nondegenerate 3-by-3 square torus is the smallest periodic two-dimensional square grid with distinct nearest neighbours in both coordinates. The 288-cycle permutation is a natural complete invariant of the original ant on that canonical board, and the 72-element physical symmetry action unexpectedly reduces all orbits to exactly eight classes. Seven of the eight periods are invisible to the previously published all-white starting-state tables. The precise finite classification supplies an interpretable, reproducible base case, while making no unsupported claim of an all-size law.
